summary: GLP-1 receptor agonist guidance genuinely reversed in late 2024 — most patients now continue rather than hold — and that's the highest-yield, most current thing to know here; the rest of the common medication classes (anticoagulants, antiplatelets, ACE-I/ARB, diuretics, metformin) each have their own hold/continue logic worth knowing before a preoperative visit.
whyThisMatters: GLP-1 perioperative guidance changed direction within about 18 months (hold → continue for most patients), which means a clinician relying on older training or an outdated institutional protocol may be giving advice that's now actively superseded — knowing the CURRENT recommendation, and why it changed, matters more than memorizing a static rule that may already be stale.
clinicalTakeaway:
GLP-1 RECEPTOR AGONISTS: as of the October 2024 ASA guidance update, MOST patients should CONTINUE their GLP-1 through elective surgery — this reversed the original June 2023 guidance to hold (daily dosing held day-of, weekly dosing held one week prior).
- Assess every patient on the day of the procedure for symptoms suggestive of delayed gastric emptying (nausea, vomiting, early satiety, abdominal distension) regardless of the hold/continue decision.
- Individualize when there's genuine concern.

For other classes:
- Anticoagulants/antiplatelets are managed per a bleeding-risk-vs-thrombosis-risk assessment specific to the procedure and the patient's indication (this is a case-by-case decision, not a blanket rule).
- ACE inhibitors/ARBs are commonly held the morning of surgery to reduce intraoperative hypotension, though outcome evidence is mixed.
- Diuretics are commonly held the morning of surgery.
- Beta-blockers and most other chronic cardiac medications are generally CONTINUED through the perioperative period to avoid rebound effects.
- Metformin is held before procedures with significant lactic acidosis risk (IV contrast, major surgery) per institutional protocol, an area of evolving practice for routine low-risk cases.

body.text: GLP-1 receptor agonists — the guidance reversed in 2024

This is a genuinely evolving area — the ASA's own guidance reversed direction in October 2024. If you learned the original 2023 'hold it' rule and haven't updated since, that recommendation has been superseded for most patients.

items: JUNE 2023 initial ASA guidance: hold daily-dosed GLP-1 agonists the day of the procedure, and hold weekly-dosed formulations for one full week before the procedure — driven by concern that GLP-1's delayed-gastric-emptying effect increases aspiration risk under anesthesia/sedation.

OCTOBER 2024 REVISED ASA guidance: reversed course — MOST patients should CONTINUE their GLP-1 receptor agonist through elective surgery. The reversal was driven by evidence that although retained gastric contents ARE significantly more common in GLP-1 users (a real, measurable finding), actual clinical pulmonary aspiration EVENTS remain low — the theoretical risk (retained contents) didn't translate into the clinical outcome (aspiration) at the rate the original guidance assumed.

Current practice: assess every patient on the day of the procedure for symptoms suggestive of delayed gastric emptying (nausea, vomiting, early satiety, abdominal bloating/distension) regardless of the hold/continue decision — a patient with active symptoms may warrant a more cautious approach (aspiration precautions, delayed elective case, or point-of-care gastric ultrasound if available) even if the general guidance favors continuing the medication.

Balance the decision against the metabolic risk of holding — bridging off a GLP-1 can be resource-intensive and risks hyperglycemia, so the decision to hold should weigh that cost against the (now better-characterized as modest) aspiration risk, rather than defaulting to hold 'to be safe' without considering the tradeoff.

rows: Commonly HELD the morning of surgery

Reduces intraoperative hypotension risk under anesthesia (these agents blunt the renin-angiotensin compensatory response); evidence on whether this changes hard outcomes is mixed, so this varies somewhat by institution/anesthesiologist preference
Commonly HELD the morning of surgery
Avoids unnecessary volume depletion and electrolyte derangement heading into a case with its own fluid shifts
Generally CONTINUED through the perioperative period, including the morning of surgery
Abrupt discontinuation risks rebound tachycardia/hypertension and myocardial ischemia — this is a 'don't stop' medication in most cases
Other chronic cardiac medications (statins, most antihypertensives not listed above)
Discontinuation risk (rebound effects, loss of a stabilizing chronic therapy) usually outweighs any perioperative benefit of holding
Individualized — a bleeding-risk-vs-thrombosis-risk decision specific to the procedure and the patient's indication for the medication

This is not a blanket rule; see the anticoagulation reversal/anticoag-labs reference content and involve the prescribing service (cardiology for a recent stent, neurology for AFib stroke prevention, etc.) for anything beyond a straightforward low-risk case
Held before procedures with significant IV contrast exposure or major surgery, per institutional protocol

Historical concern for lactic acidosis in the setting of contrast-induced or perioperative renal impairment — practice is evolving toward a more nuanced, risk-stratified approach for routine low-risk surgery rather than a blanket hold, so check current local protocol
